summary: Defines a new TLV that lets IS-IS routers flood their name to system ID mapping across the network, so people see names instead of numbers. This is an informational memo, and it was replaced by RFC 5301.

eli5.summary: Routers go by long numbers. This lets them share nicknames so humans can read them.

questions: how do is-is routers advertise names
what is a tlv in is-is
what is a system id in is-is
subtitle: A mechanism for IS-IS routers to advertise their hostnames dynamically

tldr.problem: IS-IS routers identify themselves by system IDs, which are difficult for humans to read and manage. Network administrators must manually maintain hostname-to-system ID mappings.
tldr.mechanism: The Dynamic Hostname TLV allows IS-IS routers to advertise their symbolic hostnames directly in link-state PDUs, which floods the mappings automatically across the IS-IS network.
tldr.outcome: This was replaced by RFC 5301, which provides an updated and more comprehensive mechanism for hostname distribution in IS-IS networks.

today: RFC 2763 is historic. It was replaced by RFC 5301, which standardizes hostname and router ID TLVs in IS-IS with additional features and clearer specifications.

sections.title: The Problem with System IDs
sections.content:
IS-IS routers identify themselves using a system ID, a 6 to 8 byte hexadecimal number. For network management and operations, administrators check IS-IS adjacencies, routing tables, and the link state database. Hexadecimal system IDs are difficult to read and understand compared to symbolic names.

Historically, network operators solve this by manually maintaining a table on each router that maps symbolic names to system IDs. This approach does not scale well: changing a name or adding a router requires updating configurations across the entire network.
sections.eli5: Routers have complicated number names that are hard to remember. Instead of using a phone book on every device, the routers can tell each other what their favorite names are.

sections.title: The Dynamic Hostname TLV
sections.content:
RFC 2763 defines a new TLV (Type-Length-Value) field, TLV type 137, that a router can include in its link-state PDUs. The value field contains a symbolic hostname string of 1 to 255 bytes, typically the router's fully qualified domain name (FQDN) or a subset of it.

A router may include this TLV in any fragment of its non-pseudo node LSP. When a router receives an LSP containing the Dynamic Hostname TLV, it may choose to install the hostname-to-system ID mapping in its local table. The system ID is derived from the LSP identifier itself.
sections.eli5: The TLV is like a name tag attached to each router's messages. When other routers receive the message, they can read the name tag and remember it.

sections.title: Deployment and Implementation
sections.content:
The Dynamic Hostname TLV is optional. A router can choose whether to include it in its LSP, and other routers can choose whether to use it or ignore it. There are no strict requirements on how implementations handle the TLV.

The RFC recommends using an FQDN or a subset of it as the hostname value, and notes that the string is not null-terminated. A router may also optionally include the TLV in its pseudo-node LSP to assign a symbolic name to a local LAN.
sections.eli5: Each router decides if it wants to announce its name, and each router decides if it wants to remember the names it hears. There is no requirement to use it.
